```{r setup}
library(OpenTrialDesign)
```

OpenTrialDesign supports trial planning, simulation, and reproducible analysis.
Use this guide to choose a method, assess its assumptions, and preserve the
inputs and outputs needed to replay a result.

## Installation and scope

Use R 4.5 or later. From a writable repository checkout, run
`Rscript scripts/install-product.R` to restore the lockfile and install the
package into an isolated application library. Start the browser application
with `Rscript scripts/start-product.R`. For an interactive R session started
from that checkout, activate the same library with
`source("scripts/product-library.R")` and `activate_product_library()`.

For an existing R library with the package dependencies installed, use
`R CMD INSTALL OpenTrialDesign_0.4.1.tar.gz` with the verified release archive.
Install the relevant optional engines for the intended workflows. The browser
interface requires Shiny, HTML reporting requires rmarkdown and Pandoc, and
PDF reporting additionally requires LaTeX. The repository's Docker image
provides the application and reporting tools.

The supported designs include fixed normal and binary superiority,
normal-means designs with unequal allocation and superiority, noninferiority,
or equivalence objectives, one-sided group sequential and two-stage adaptive
normal designs, exponential proportional-hazards planning and simulation,
and piecewise-exponential nonproportional-hazards simulation. Choose the
specific adapter whose assumptions match the proposed trial. Cluster,
recurrent-event, and competing-risk designs are outside the supported scope.

## Specify the scientific question

`trial_spec()` records endpoint, treatment minus control effect, sidedness,
total alpha, target power and equal allocation. Positive and negative effects
must agree with a directional alternative. No default margin is inferred.

```{r fixed}
spec <- trial_spec(effect = 0.5, sd = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
sample_size(spec)
trial_power(spec, 64)
```

The normal calculation uses `stats::power.t.test` for independent normal
observations with a common variance, and includes rejection in both tails
for two-sided power (`strict = TRUE`). Binary planning uses
`stats::power.prop.test` without continuity correction. Sample size is rounded
up per arm and analytical power recalculated at that integer size. All reported
sizes are evaluable participants; no hidden attrition inflation is applied.

```{r binary}
binary <- trial_spec("binary", effect = 0.15, p_control = 0.3)
sample_size(binary)
compare_scenarios(list(base = spec, smaller_effect = trial_spec(effect = 0.3)))
```

## Monte Carlo operating characteristics

Analytical power differs from a Monte Carlo estimate. Each simulation result
contains the rejection count, replication count, seed, estimate, plug-in MCSE
`sqrt(p_hat * (1-p_hat) / B)`, and exact Clopper-Pearson 95% interval. A zero
MCSE at zero observed rejections does not imply absence of uncertainty; use the
interval. Expected enrollment, information, event-count and duration summaries
include approximate t-based Monte Carlo intervals. Stopping and target-attainment
probabilities use marginal exact binomial intervals; they do not have simultaneous
95% coverage. Choose replication counts for the precision required: at true error
0.025, 1000 replications give an approximate MCSE of 0.00494.

```{r simulation}
simulate_trial(spec, 64, nsim = 200, seed = 2026)
simulate_trial(spec, 64, nsim = 200, seed = 2026, null = TRUE)
```

The equality null uses treatment effect zero, not the planning alternative.
The normal test is the pooled t test. The default binary analysis uses
`prop.test` without continuity correction. A conditional Fisher test is
available as an explicit simulation option. All-zero or all-one binary samples cannot reject
equality and are assigned p=1. Discreteness can affect nominal type I error.
The equality null alone does not establish uniform control across all nuisance
parameters. Broader null grids and multiplicity control are study-specific work.

## Sequential designs and stopping

```{r sequential}
if (requireNamespace("gsDesign", quietly = TRUE)) {
  seq_design <- sequential_design(information = c(0.33, 0.67, 1),
                                  futility = "nonbinding")
  print(seq_design)
  plot_design(seq_design)
  sequential_power(seq_design, theta = 0)
  conditional_power(seq_design, z = 1.5)
  simulate_sequential(seq_design, nsim = 200, seed = 2026)
}
```

Sequential alpha is the **one-sided upper efficacy** error. A lower futility
crossing does not reject the null. For gsDesign, no-futility uses test.type=1,
binding beta-spending uses 3, and nonbinding beta-spending uses 4. Beta spending
is Hwang-Shih-DeCani with gamma=-2. Nonbinding upper boundaries protect alpha
if futility is ignored; power and expected information depend on whether
futility is followed. The canonical simulator can evaluate that distinction,
and refuses to ignore a binding rule. Analytical gsProbability enforces lower
stopping even for a design calibrated with nonbinding futility.

Information fractions are prespecified. The canonical simulation is a Brownian
independent-increments experiment, not patient-level evidence for arbitrary
endpoints or data-dependent information times. `theta` is canonical drift;
the default analytical alternative is the native design's drift. Information
is normalized to fixed-design information, not a patient count.

The rpact adapter returns its own native object. Engine-specific OF and Pocock
spending approximations are retained. Never transfer boundaries, power values,
or information scales between engines without an explicit compatibility check.

## Adaptive sample size recalculation

```{r adaptive}
if (requireNamespace("rpact", quietly = TRUE)) {
  adaptive <- adaptive_simulation(nsim = 200, seed = 2026)
  print(adaptive)
}
```

This workflow uses rpact's `getDesignInverseNormal` and `getSimulationMeans`
with native conditional-power recalculation. The combination weights are fixed
by the originally planned information fractions. Stage-one enrollment is total
across both arms, and stage-two limits are additional enrollment across both
arms. Native normal-approximation recalculations can yield fractional effective
sample sizes; these simulations are not an integer operational enrollment rule. Independent normally distributed stage observations, equal allocation,
and the rpact normal approximation are assumed. Null and alternative scenarios
are always reported. There is no futility boundary in this adapter. The
procedure does not authorize changing an ordinary pooled-test design after
observing an unblinded effect. Confirmatory use requires protocol-specific
review of combination weights, independent stage p-values and the adaptation
rule; a finite Monte Carlo experiment alone does not prove error control.

## Survival planning and simulation

```{r survival}
if (requireNamespace("rpact", quietly = TRUE)) {
  surv_design <- survival_design(hazard_ratio = 0.7, median_control = 12,
    accrual = 18, followup = 12, dropout = 0.1)
  print(surv_design$data$native)
}
if (requireNamespace("simsurv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  simulate_survival(100, events = 120, nsim = 20, seed = 2026)
}
```

The estimand is the treatment/control hazard ratio. Planning supports HR below
one as benefit. The Schoenfeld approximation supplies the event target, and
rpact translates that target into enrollment under uniform accrual, exponential
survival, equal allocation and independent dropout. The returned native sizes
are unrounded planning quantities; round enrollment and event targets upward
when specifying an operational trial, then assess the resulting operating
characteristics with the simulation API. No precision claim is made for
unmodeled recruitment patterns or nonproportional hazards.

Simulation uses simsurv event times, independent exponential dropout and
administrative censoring. All durations use one common unit. `dropout` is a
probability by `dropout_time`, not a hazard. The logrank signed treatment
observed-minus-expected score supports benefit when negative. The p-value is
lower-tail one-sided. If an event target is supplied, the trial stops at that
calendar event or the administrative cap, whichever comes first. The result
reports target attainment; it never assumes an unreachable event target was
met. Participants not recruited by early stopping do not enter the analysis.

## Reports, diagnostics and application

```{r diagnostics}
diagnose_design(simulate_trial(spec, 64, nsim = 50, seed = 2026))
```

`render_report(result, "report.html")` writes results, native engine output,
assumptions, methods, versions, RNG details, seed and validation status.
`render_report(result, "report.pdf", "pdf")` additionally needs LaTeX.
`run_app()` launches the optional Shiny interface; calculations use this same
public API. App actions trigger calculations explicitly. Results must be
recomputed after changing inputs. The report selector chooses among the
previously computed result objects.

## Example library and scientific verification

The installed `examples/catalog.csv` documents 30 independently executable
scenarios; installed `examples/ASSUMPTIONS.md` explains each rationale and
limits the synthetic effects to teaching/planning demonstrations. They are
accessible through `run_example("TD-001")` and standalone scripts.
The supplied repository contained no external plan defining TD IDs. This
version defines its own explicit product catalog; equivalence to that missing
external specification is not claimed.

Numerical reference checks compare normal/binary calculations directly to
stats, sequential spending and power to engine integration, and survival events
to the Schoenfeld expression. These verify adapter behavior, not independent
validation of their engines. Monte Carlo checks use prespecified seeds and
tolerances scaled to sampling error. A reference expectation is never replaced
with a simulated point estimate merely to obtain passing tests.

See repository `validation/` for actual execution logs and `docs/PHASE-STATUS.md`
for limitations. No result should be described as scientifically validated
solely because a function returned successfully. rpact installation
qualification for GxP environments is separate and has not been performed here.

## Portable projects and batch replay

```{r projects}
project <- trial_project("fixed_sample_size", list(effect = 0.5), "Demonstration")
execute_project(project)
```

Projects freeze all default parameters and record schema and software versions.
`write_project(project, "design.json")` saves non-executable JSON.
`execute_project(read_project("design.json"))` replays it through the same core.
Schema validation rejects unknown workflows, arguments, code-like numeric
values and unsupported versions. Scientific input validation occurs in the
engine when executed. JSON is configuration data; no R expressions from an
import are evaluated. Only trusted local archival RDS files should be loaded
by the user outside the application.

Supported workflows are `fixed_sample_size`, `fixed_power`, `fixed_simulation`,
`sequential_design`, `sequential_means`, `adaptive_simulation`, `survival_design`
and `survival_simulation`. Fixed workflows take trial_spec parameters plus
sample size and simulation settings as applicable. Other workflows take the
corresponding public function's parameters.

## Operational sequential enrollment

```{r sequential-enrollment}
if (requireNamespace("rpact", quietly=TRUE)) sequential_sample_size()
```

This positive-mean, one-sided, equal-allocation workflow uses rpact's native
t-approximation planning and power functions. Cumulative per-arm stage sizes
are rounded upward, the information fractions recomputed, and spending
boundaries recalibrated in rpact. The maximum size is increased if recalculated
power falls below target. Final output includes integer stage counts, realized
information and achieved analytical power. No gsDesign boundaries or fixed
stats t-test calculations are combined with this procedure.

## Background jobs and reproducibility exports

`start_simulation(project)` starts an isolated process for a fixed, adaptive or
survival simulation project. `simulation_status(job)` is nonblocking;
`collect_simulation(job)` requires successful completion. `cancel_simulation(job)`
terminates an active worker and never returns a partial estimate as a completed
run. The application allows one active job per session and remains interactive
while it runs. Closing the session cancels its worker. API users can choose
larger runs than the application's 100,000-replication limit.

`result_table(result)` provides spreadsheet data. `export_bundle(result,
"trial.zip", include_report = FALSE)` writes CSV, assumptions, provenance,
session information, the exact result, the replay project when present and
MD5 integrity checks. MD5 checks detect accidental changes, not authenticity.
Use the Projects and exports tab to save JSON, CSV and ZIP, and Scientific
reporting for HTML/PDF. The full guide is downloadable from the application.

See the repository deployment guide for local, container and batch commands.
The version-1 example catalog is now explicitly defined by the installed
catalog and per-example rationales. It does not claim equivalence to an absent
external project plan. These workflows support planning and simulation within
the stated assumptions; they do not confer protocol-specific qualification.


## Scientific review before execution

`review_project(project)` displays the exact estimand, hypothesis direction,
alpha definition, allocation, nuisance assumptions, stopping and simulation
settings. It does not run simulations or confer scientific validation. The app
shows the live review before execution; calculated outputs retain their frozen
click-time specification even if inputs are later edited.

## Sensitivity analysis and batch simulation

```{r}
projects <- scenario_grid(trial_project(),
  list(effect=c(.3,.5),power=c(.8,.9)))
comparison <- run_scenarios(projects)
comparison$data$summary
```

Any supported project can be executed in a batch; the grid helper varies scalar
parameters. Simulation seeds increment deterministically by row unless
`seed_strategy="preserve"` is explicitly selected. Explicitly varying seeds
requires preserve. Reusing seeds does not establish independence between
scenario estimates. Information vectors require constructing separate projects.

Use `start_scenarios(projects)`, `simulation_status(job)`,
`collect_simulation(job)` and `cancel_simulation(job)` for asynchronous work.
A cancelled run has no completed partial result. Errors abort by default;
`continue_on_error=TRUE` retains failures separately, never as scientific
estimates. Each successful result retains its engine and complete provenance.
Monte Carlo confidence intervals are marginal, with no simultaneous coverage
or inferential combination across engines.

`export_bundle(comparison,"sensitivity.zip",include_report=FALSE)` includes all
scenario JSON projects, a filename-to-scenario index, failures, results and
integrity checks. The app supports up to 36 fixed-design grid scenarios and
100,000 total simulation replications; the R grid helper permits up to 1000
scenarios. Larger scientific experiments should plan precision and resources
explicitly.

## Extended verification and external review

The prespecified stress script evaluates 40 scenarios: normal small/large sample
sizes and both directions, binary nuisance risks from .01 to .99, sequential
spending and binding/nonbinding futility, survival dropout/event/calendar stops,
and bounded native adaptive resizing. It reports estimates, MCSE, exact binomial
intervals and a five-theoretical-MCSE screening band. Reference gates compare
matched procedures. Sparse binary and low-event logrank cases are diagnostics;
departures are retained and are not relabelled as exact calibration.

Passing a finite grid does not establish uniform type I error control. Independent
scientific review, real-user usability evaluation and external TD-plan mapping
have not been performed. Reproducible protocols, blank observation forms and
review criteria are supplied in docs/review of the source repository.


## Sparse binary counts and explicit exact-test simulation

```{r}
sparse <- trial_spec("binary",effect=.005,p_control=.01)
binary_diagnostics(sparse,10,null=TRUE)
```

The count threshold of five is only a heuristic. Historical score-test examples
are downloadable in the app and installed validation folder. Use
`simulate_trial(sparse,10,nsim=1000,seed=42,null=TRUE,binary_test="fisher")`
to explicitly evaluate a conditional Fisher test. Its conservatism can reduce
power. Approximate sample sizing remains separate; increasing the simulation
count cannot repair miscalibration. Results and reports retain this distinction.

## Unequal normal allocation and clinical margin tests

```{r}
if(requireNamespace("rpact",quietly=TRUE)){
  ni <- means_design(allocation_ratio=2,margin=.3,effect=0)
  ni$data[c("n_control","n_treatment","rejection_probability")]
}
if(requireNamespace("PowerTOST",quietly=TRUE)){
  eq <- means_design(hypothesis="equivalence",effect=.02,lower=-.2,upper=.4,allocation_ratio=2)
  eq$data[c("n_control","n_treatment","rejection_probability")]
}
```

Effects and margins are treatment minus control in original response units.
For higher-is-better NI, H0 is delta <= -margin; for lower-is-better it is delta
>= margin. Margin values in these examples are synthetic and must not be adopted
without clinical justification. TOST equivalence is the intersection of two
one-sided rejections; global level is alpha, not twice alpha. Its matching CI
has coverage 1-2*alpha. Nonsignificance is not equivalence.

`simulate_means_design()` evaluates NI at the null margin or equivalence at
both boundary nulls, plus the specified alternative. Use actual arm sizes.
For fixed-size analytical evaluation, supply n_control and n_treatment to
means_design. At a null effect the result reports rejection_probability and
leaves achieved_power missing, rather than labelling type I error as power.
The exact equivalence engine assumes independent parallel groups and common
normal variance; crossover or binary equivalence is not supported here.

## Nonproportional survival profiles

```{r,eval=FALSE}
simulate_nonph(times=c(0,6),lambda_control=c(.06,.06),
  lambda_treatment=c(.08,.03),n_total=240,events=100,
  allocation_treatment=2,allocation_control=1,nsim=1000,seed=42)
```

This uses native rpact piecewise-exponential simulation and ordinary one-sided
logrank analysis. Intervals are follow-up times; the final interval is unbounded.
The supplied profile crosses from higher to lower treatment hazards. No constant
HR or uniform survival dominance is inferred. Recruitment is uniform; there is
no additional administrative follow-up cap. A failed event target aborts the
adapter instead of omitting trials. The equal-curve null is checked separately.

Vary enrollment/events in explicit complete projects to evaluate simulation-based
planning under non-PH. Never apply the older PH Schoenfeld planner to these
profiles. All new workflows support JSON, reporting, scenario batches and
cancellable workers. See docs/METHOD-EXTENSIONS.md in the repository for exact
scope and the four-theoretical-MCSE scientific reference criteria.

## References

Schoenfeld DA (1981). The asymptotic properties of nonparametric tests for
comparing survival distributions. *Biometrika*, 68, 316-319.

Lan KKG, DeMets DL (1983). Discrete sequential boundaries for clinical trials.
*Biometrika*, 70, 659-663.

Hwang IK, Shih WJ, DeCani JS (1990). Group sequential designs using a family
of type I error probability spending functions. *Statistics in Medicine*, 9,
1439-1445.

Lehmacher W, Wassmer G (1999). Adaptive sample size calculations in group
sequential trials. *Biometrics*, 55, 1286-1290.

Brilleman SL, Wolfe R, Moreno-Betancur M, Crowther MJ (2021). Simulating
survival data using the simsurv R package. *Journal of Statistical Software*,
97(3), 1-27. Use `citation("rpact")`, `citation("gsDesign")`,
`citation("survival")` and `citation("simsurv")` for current engine citations.
